concepts.name: Gandhi's Philosophy on Women's Participation in NCM
key_dimensions: Gandhi's belief in women's moral superiority and capacity for non-violent resistance
How NCM marked a shift from women as passive supporters to active political agents
Gandhi's deliberate mobilization strategy vs. spontaneous women's participation
Contradiction: Gandhi's simultaneous reinforcement of domestic roles while encouraging public activism

concepts.name: Sarojini Naidu's Role in the Non-Cooperation Movement
key_dimensions: Her position as one of the first prominent women leaders at the national organizational level
Role in picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops alongside male leaders
Her oratory as a tool of mass mobilization — 'Nightingale of India' in political context
Distinction between her role in NCM vs. later Civil Disobedience Movement (trap: don't conflate the two)

concepts.name: Boycott of Foreign Cloth and Liquor Shops: Women as Primary Agents
key_dimensions: Women's specific assignment in picketing — rationale behind targeting these venues
Social significance: women traditionally associated with household purchasing, making their boycott symbolically powerful
Geographic spread — participation from urban upper-caste women vs. regional variations
Trap: NCM picketing by women was largely peaceful and symbolic vs. the more confrontational tactics in later movements

concepts.name: Promotion of Khadi and Swadeshi by Women
key_dimensions: Spinning charkha as a political act — women integrating domestic space with nationalist resistance
Gandhi's deliberate use of charkha to include women across class and caste lines
Khadi as a unifying symbol: how it bridged urban educated women and rural women
Trap: Swadeshi movement (1905) had limited women's participation vs. NCM's broader inclusion — key distinction

concepts.name: Role of Women in Tilak's and Gandhi's Contrasting Mobilization Models
key_dimensions: Bal Gangadhar Tilak's use of religious festivals (Ganesh Utsav) — limited formal role for women
Gandhi's NCM as a conscious departure: explicitly inviting women into public political space
Shift from cultural nationalism (masculine) to moral nationalism (inclusive of women)
How this distinction is tested: 'Who first brought women into mainstream nationalist politics?'

concepts.name: Bi-Directional Impact: NCM's Effect on Women's Social Emancipation
key_dimensions: Did political participation translate into social equality? — the critical debate
NCM participation raising women's consciousness but Gandhi's framework still confining them to 'feminine virtues'
Post-NCM: emergence of women's organizations (e.g., All India Women's Conference, 1927) — causal link
Trap: NCM participation ≠ formal political rights — don't conflate mobilization with suffrage or legal emancipation

concepts.name: Basanti Devi and Regional Women Leaders in Bengal
key_dimensions: Basanti Devi's arrest during NCM — significance as one of the first high-profile arrests of women
Her role in picketing and selling khadi in Calcutta
How Bengal's women leaders operated within a male-dominated Congress structure
Distinction: Basanti Devi in NCM vs. her continued activism in later movements — chronological trap

concepts.name: Women's Participation in Hartals and Strikes
key_dimensions: Nature of women's participation in hartals — moral pressure vs. physical participation
Role in ensuring male family members adhered to strike calls — domestic enforcement of political discipline
Class dimension: upper/middle-class women in hartals vs. working-class women's different forms of resistance
Geographic variation: Punjab, Bengal, and UP showing different intensities of women's hartal participation

concepts.name: Arrest and Imprisonment of Women During NCM
key_dimensions: NCM saw relatively fewer women's arrests compared to Civil Disobedience Movement — important comparative fact
Significance of Basanti Devi's arrest as a turning point in public perception
British colonial response to arresting women: reluctance due to fear of public backlash
Trap: Mass arrest of women is more associated with CDM (1930) and Quit India (1942), not NCM — a frequent UPSC trap

concepts.name: Role of Women in the Khilafat-NCM Confluence
key_dimensions: How Muslim women participated in the combined Khilafat-NCM agitation
Bi Amma (Abadi Bano Begum) — mother of the Ali Brothers — as a symbol of Muslim women's activism
Significance: purdah-observing women entering public space for the first time as a political statement
Trap: Khilafat movement's women's participation was distinct in character (religious motivation) vs. nationalist motivation in Congress women

concepts.name: Bi Amma (Abadi Bano Begum): Pioneer of Muslim Women's Activism
key_dimensions: Her role in the Khilafat-NCM as a public speaker despite purdah observance
Symbolic importance: an older, purdah-observing woman addressing mixed public gatherings
How her activism challenged colonial stereotypes about Indian Muslim women
Distinction: Her motivation (Khilafat/religious) vs. Hindu women's motivation in NCM (nationalist) — often tested as a contrast

concepts.name: Class and Caste Dimensions of Women's Participation in NCM
key_dimensions: Predominantly upper-caste, educated, urban women in formal NCM activities
Limited participation of lower-caste and rural women in the organized movement
Gandhi's attempt to bridge class divide through khadi but structural limitations
Critical angle: whether NCM truly democratized women's political participation or remained elite-dominated

concepts.name: Women's Organizations as Precursors and Products of NCM Participation
key_dimensions: Seva Samitis and Mahila Mandals formed during NCM for organizational support
How NCM experience led to formal women's organizations post-1920s (AIWC 1927)
Role of Annie Besant's Home Rule League in preparing organizational ground for women (pre-NCM context)
Trap: Annie Besant was more prominent in Home Rule League (1916) — her NCM role was limited and she was critical of Gandhi's methods

concepts.name: Annie Besant's Position on the Non-Cooperation Movement
key_dimensions: Besant's opposition to Gandhi's NCM — she feared chaos and mob violence
Her contrasting approach: constitutional methods vs. Gandhi's mass civil disobedience
Significance: A prominent woman leader opposing NCM — complicates the narrative of universal women's support
Trap: Besant is often associated with women in freedom struggle broadly, but she was AGAINST NCM specifically — a classic UPSC trap

concepts.name: Role of Women in Student Boycott and National Schools During NCM
key_dimensions: Women's role in encouraging family members (sons, husbands) to boycott government schools
Emergence of women as teachers in national schools set up as alternatives
How educational boycott expanded women's public role as educators and mentors
Limitation: Women's own education was still secondary — the boycott affected men's institutions primarily

concepts.name: Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay's Early Activism and NCM
key_dimensions: Her early political awakening during NCM period
Later prominence in CDM distinguished from her formative NCM participation — chronological clarity needed
Her advocacy for integrating women's rights with nationalist politics
Trap: Kamaladevi is more prominently associated with CDM and post-independence cultural work — her NCM role is formative but secondary

concepts.name: Suspension of NCM (Chauri Chaura, 1922) and Its Effect on Women's Mobilization
key_dimensions: Gandhi's unilateral suspension of NCM after Chauri Chaura violence — impact on momentum of women's participation
Women leaders' reactions to the suspension — largely supportive of Gandhi's decision
How the suspension created a political vacuum that women's organizations partially filled
Critical question: Did the suspension set back women's political mobilization or consolidate organizational structures?

concepts.name: Comparative Participation: Women in NCM vs. Civil Disobedience Movement
key_dimensions: NCM: Predominantly symbolic participation (picketing, khadi, boycott support) with fewer arrests
CDM (1930): Far larger numbers, direct action (salt march participation, forest satyagraha), mass arrests
Qualitative shift: CDM saw women as frontline protesters, not just supporters — NCM was transitional
Trap: UPSC often asks about 'first time' women entered political arena — answer is NCM, but mass participation peak was CDM

concepts.name: Symbolic vs. Structural Participation: Limits of Women's Role in NCM
key_dimensions: Women occupied peripheral roles in Congress decision-making despite frontline activism
Gandhi's framework: valorized women's participation but within 'feminine' virtues of sacrifice and suffering
No significant women in top Congress leadership positions during NCM (unlike later CDM and Quit India)
Critical historiographical debate: Was NCM a genuine turning point for women's emancipation or a controlled mobilization?

concepts.name: Press, Propaganda, and Women's Voice During NCM
key_dimensions: Role of nationalist newspapers in publishing women's speeches, arrests, and activities
Women writers and journalists using print media to spread NCM ideology
Gandhi's Young India and Navajivan as platforms that addressed women readers and participants
Limitation: Most women activists were reported upon rather than being authors — passive representation vs. active voice
